lines.trans: On the one hand, I work in a cool restaurant.
And on the other hand, you eat ordinary sausages.
Our chef cooks the most delicious food.
But total chaos always reigns in the kitchen.
Guests think this is the most peaceful place.
They will never know the truth about us.
Every customer considers themselves an important person.
And we simply pour them wine.
Work in the kitchen is very hard and nerve-wracking.
On the other hand, it's never boring here!
Our morning shift is starting soon.
Then prepare for a new workday!
I will prove to the chef that I know how to cook.

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'and', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('so, and what about') (starting a question: а жвачку?) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

бывать.gloss: to happen, to be (sometimes); to visit

meanings.en: to happen, to exist, there can be
meanings.note: 3rd person бывает = there is / can be
Secondary conversational sense ('to visit, to be at') (часто бывать где-то) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: У мужчины бывает не только жена.
examples.trans: A man can have more than just a wife.

examples.text: У мужчины, мальчик, бывает не только жена. Это моя девушка.
examples.trans: A man, my boy, can have more than just a wife. She's my girlfriend.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'in' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('into, to') (+ accusative (where to)) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('important').

examples.text: Я тебе утром говорил: не торопись. Это очень важный вопрос.
examples.trans: I told you this morning: don't rush. It's a very important question.

meanings.note: Common neuter noun meaning 'wine' in everyday Russian.
Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('tasty, delicious').

examples.trans: The bread rings are very tasty.

examples.text: Марина Сергеевна, присядьте. Попробуйте чай с сушками, очень вкусные.
examples.trans: Marina Sergeyevna, have a seat. Try the tea with bread rings, they're very tasty.

meanings.note: Prefix 'вс-' ('up') marks upward or sudden onset of action (stem 'егда').

examples.trans: She's offended. She's always like that.

meanings.note: Abstract masculine noun formed with the productive Slavic suffix '-ость', denoting the quality or state of 'guest'.

examples.trans: All the guests love them very much.

examples.text: Сегодня вечером к нам придут гости.
examples.trans: Guests are coming to our place tonight.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to cook; to prepare', paired with 'приготовить'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to prepare') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Я уже не могу готовить, стирать, убирать. Я хочу на море!
examples.trans: I can't take the cooking, washing and cleaning any more. I want to go to the sea!

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to prepare', forming an aspectual pair with 'приготовиться'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense. The reflexive suffix '-ся'/'-сь' makes the action intransitive, reciprocal, or directed at the subject.

examples.trans: We are simply preparing for the morning show.
The students were preparing for the exam.
And little Grisha is preparing for the morning show.

meanings.note: на днях = in the next few days, or the other day

examples.trans: I'll call in the next few days.
Any day now, on the website.

meanings.note: что и требовалось доказать = Q.E.D., which is what needed to be proved

examples.trans: There, which is what needed to be proved!

examples.text: Я обязательно докажу своё кулинарное мастерство.
examples.trans: I will definitely prove my culinary mastery.

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('other, another, different').
Secondary conversational sense ('different') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Послушайте, а можно в другое место? Здесь плохо пахнет.
examples.trans: Listen, could we go somewhere else? It smells bad in here.

meanings.note: думать о + prepositional = to think about

examples.trans: I have no time to think about that.

examples.text: Мне некогда об этом думать. Слишком много дел.
examples.trans: I have no time to think about that. There's too much to do.

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'food', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: В этом ресторане всегда свежая еда.
examples.trans: There is always fresh food in this restaurant.
Oh no, bad food? Does your stomach hurt?

meanings.note: not to be confused with есть 'there is' (from быть)

examples.text: Я вчера ел маринованные грибы. Может, один гриб был плохой.
examples.trans: Yesterday I ate pickled mushrooms. Maybe one mushroom was bad.

зато.gloss: but on the other hand, to make up for it

meanings.en: but on the other hand, at least
meanings.note: introduces a compensating positive fact

examples.text: Четыре по алгебре, зато по физкультуре пятёрка.
examples.trans: A four in algebra, but a five in gym.
The flat is small, but at least it's in the centre.

examples.text: Ничего страшного. Сейчас зато аппетит нагуляем.
examples.trans: No big deal. At least we'll walk up an appetite now.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'here'.
emphasis: вот поэтому ты и... = that's exactly why you...

examples.trans: I was born and grew up here.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'to' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.

examples.trans: There's someone here to see you.

examples.text: Аркадий Борисович, извините, тут к вам человек.
examples.trans: Arkady Borisovich, I'm sorry, there's a man here to see you.

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'every', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.

examples.text: Аркаш, мне москвичи звонят каждый день. Может, всё-таки передумаем?
examples.trans: Arkasha, the people from Moscow call me every day. Maybe we should reconsider after all?

meanings.note: постоянный клиент = regular customer

examples.trans: I'm working with clients right now.
This is only for regular clients.

examples.text: Извините, пожалуйста, я сейчас работаю с клиентами.
examples.trans: Excuse me, please, I'm working with clients right now.

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'cool', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.
Secondary conversational sense ('steep, sharp') (literal) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Раз ты такой крутой, познакомь нас!
examples.trans: Since you're so cool, introduce us!

examples.text: Ну раз ты такой крутой, может, познакомишь нас?
examples.trans: Well, since you're so cool, maybe you'll introduce us?

meanings.note: Entered Russian via Polish 'kuchnia' and Middle High German 'küchen', ultimately from Late Latin 'coquina' (from 'coquere', to cook).
Secondary conversational sense ('cuisine, cooking') (русская кухня = Russian cuisine) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Three rooms and a big kitchen.
And the kitchen is over there.

meanings.note: in 'рабочее место' = workplace, job
Secondary conversational sense ('post, position') (на его место = in his place) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Давай мы его уволим, а тебя на его место назначим.
examples.trans: Let's fire him and put you in his place.

meanings.note: нас = us (gen/acc/prep); у нас = we have, at our place
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
examples.trans: Look, how dirty our toilet is!

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'on' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('onto, to; for') (+ accusative: на второй срок) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: The programme is on the website.
He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: + dative of the person, + accusative of the drink

examples.text: Ты мне сейчас водку наливаешь, да?
examples.trans: Right now you're pouring me vodka, aren't you?

meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'чинаться'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to begin', forming an aspectual pair with 'начаться'. The reflexive suffix '-ся'/'-сь' makes the action intransitive, reciprocal, or directed at the subject.

examples.text: Спасибо, теперь для нас начинается новая жизнь.
examples.trans: Thank you, now a new life begins for us.
Our work is only just beginning.

meanings.note: наш, наша, наше, наши; agrees with the noun

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: goes right before the word it negates
Qualitative or relational adjective formed with the productive '-н-' suffix, meaning 'nervous' and agreeing in gender, number, and case.

examples.trans: Do you have a nervous tic?

examples.text: Работа на кухне очень трудная и нервная.
examples.trans: Work in the kitchen is very hard and nerve-wracking.

meanings.note: used with не before the verb, or alone

examples.text: Я никогда не был на море.
examples.trans: I've never been to the sea.

examples.text: Я никогда в жизни не пробовал такой вкусной утки!
examples.trans: I have never in my life tasted such delicious duck!

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'but', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо ещё.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need more.
I want to, but I can't.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо сделать ещё больше.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need to do even more.

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('new').

examples.text: Ну что, довольна? Теперь новую работу искать.
examples.trans: Well, happy now? Now I have to look for a new job.

meanings.note: + prepositional; об before a vowel: об этом

examples.text: Мне некогда об этом думать. Слишком много дел.
examples.trans: I have no time to think about that. There's too much to do.

meanings.note: Prefix 'об-' ('around, about') marks encirclement or comprehensive action (stem 'ычный'). Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('ordinary, usual').

examples.text: Да нет на него никакого компромата. Обычный мужик.
examples.trans: There is no compromising material on him at all. Just an ordinary guy.

examples.text: Я просто пошла на обычный концерт.
examples.trans: I simply went to an ordinary concert.

meanings.note: agrees in gender and case with the noun
Secondary conversational sense ('alone') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('they') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.

examples.text: Ты преподавай. А они пусть строят свои торговые центры.
examples.trans: You teach. And let them build their shopping centres.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'very'.
Secondary conversational sense ('very much') (with verbs: очень люблю) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I love our town very much.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Qualitative or relational adjective formed with the productive '-н-' suffix, meaning 'full' and agreeing in gender, number, and case.
Secondary conversational sense ('complete, total, utter') (полный кошмар = a total nightmare) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: На столе стоял полный стакан воды.
examples.trans: A full glass of water stood on the table.

examples.text: Ну что я тебе скажу, Аркаша? Это полный кошмар!
examples.trans: Well, what can I tell you, Arkasha? This is a total nightmare!

meanings.note: as a side word: Правда, всё нормально = Honestly, everything's fine
as a side word: Правда, всё нормально = Honestly, everything's fine

examples.text: Правда, Нин, всё нормально. Скажи что-нибудь, пожалуйста.
examples.trans: Honestly, Nina, everything's fine. Say something, please.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'just'.
Secondary conversational sense ('easy') (это просто = it's easy) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Мы просто не хотели вас беспокоить. Всё отменим!
examples.trans: We just didn't want to bother you. We'll cancel it all!

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'work', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('job') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
работать + instrumental = to work as: работать мэром

examples.text: Я уже четыре года работаю мэром.
examples.trans: I've been working as mayor for four years now.

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'working', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.
Secondary conversational sense ('worker') (as a noun) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Мы построим кластер. Это тысячи рабочих мест.
examples.trans: We will build the cluster. That means thousands of jobs.

meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'restaurant' (from 'restaurer', to restore strength with rich broth); entered Russian in the early 19th century.

examples.text: Слушай, Нина, это же тот самый ресторан!
examples.trans: Listen, Nina, this is that very restaurant!

examples.text: Мы рады видеть вас в нашем ресторане.
examples.trans: We are glad to see you in our restaurant.
They called from the Italian restaurant.

meanings.note: + instrumental; со before some consonant clusters: со всеми

examples.trans: Share it all equally with everyone, understand?

meanings.note: forms the superlative: самый главный = the most important
Secondary conversational sense ('the very') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: The most important thing is the people.
Do you know the main thing?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('oneself') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.

examples.text: А с Пашей я снова чувствую себя женщиной.
examples.trans: And with Pasha I feel like a woman again.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'коро'). Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.text: Так, не шумим. Я скоро вернусь.
examples.trans: Right, no noise. I'll be back soon.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'кучно'). Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.text: Я не люблю детей. С ними скучно.
examples.trans: I do not like children. It is boring with them.

examples.text: Зато здесь никогда не бывает скучно!
examples.trans: On the other hand, it's never boring here!

meanings.note: morning or afternoon shift at school or work

examples.trans: We're on the afternoon shift today.

examples.text: А у нас сегодня вторая смена.
examples.trans: We're on the afternoon shift today.

meanings.note: Derived feminine noun formed with a productive Slavic suffix, used in spoken Russian to mean 'sausage'.

examples.text: А с другой стороны, ты ешь обычные сосиски.
examples.trans: And on the other hand, you eat ordinary sausages.

meanings.note: Qualitative or relational adjective formed with the productive '-н-' suffix, meaning 'calm' and agreeing in gender, number, and case.
Secondary conversational sense ('good (night)') (спокойной ночи = good night) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Это ваша самоуверенность промелькнула. Спокойной ночи!
examples.trans: That was your overconfidence flashing by. Good night!

meanings.note: с другой стороны = on the other hand
Secondary conversational sense ('direction') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: On the other hand, it's interesting.
The shop is on that side.

examples.text: Бред какой-то. Но, с другой стороны, чем я рискую?
examples.trans: What nonsense. But on the other hand, what have I got to lose?

считать.gloss: to count; to think, to consider

meanings.note: посчитать / сосчитать are the perfectives
Secondary conversational sense ('to consider, to believe') (я считаю, что... = I think that...) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Эх, Паша, Паша. Ты считать не умеешь.
examples.trans: Oh, Pasha, Pasha. You can't count.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'then'.
Secondary conversational sense ('then, in that case') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Я тебе тогда сказал: ты меня ещё поцелуешь.
examples.trans: I told you back then: you'll kiss me one day.

meanings.note: Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('difficult, hard').

examples.text: Детство у меня было трудное. Я вырос в коммуналке.
examples.trans: My childhood was hard. I grew up in a communal flat.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('you') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'знать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to recognise; to find out', paired with 'узнавать'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to find out, to learn') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I'll find out where he is.
You recognised me. Thanks for seeing me.

уметь.gloss: to know how to, to be able to

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'меть'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to know how to', forming an aspectual pair with 'суметь'.

examples.text: Эх, Паша, Паша. Ты считать не умеешь.
examples.trans: Oh, Pasha, Pasha. You can't count.

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'тренний'). Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('morning').

examples.trans: Our morning shift is starting soon.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'chaos, disarray' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Но на кухне всегда царит полный хаос.
examples.trans: But total chaos always reigns in the kitchen.

examples.text: Без вашего участия на кухне наступит хаос.
examples.trans: Without your participation, chaos will break out in the kitchen.

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to reign'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.text: Но на кухне всегда царит полный хаос.
examples.trans: But total chaos always reigns in the kitchen.

meanings.note: the plural is a different word: люди, людям, о людях
Secondary conversational sense ('people') (plural люди, a different word) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: There are a lot of people here.
I know the problems of ordinary people.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('what') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('that') (conjunction) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('? = well?') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'chef' (head, leader, from Latin 'caput'); in Russian kitchen culture 'шеф' is the standard form of address for the executive head chef.

examples.trans: The chef is in the kitchen.

meanings.note: pointing at a thing or a situation; 'это' + noun = 'this is ...'
points at something: это моё = that's mine
Secondary conversational sense ('is') (linking word: главное — это народ) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: And this is for you. A toy car!

meanings.note: меня = me (genitive/accusative), мне = to me (dative)
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
